name: publisher-subscriber
intent: Decouple event producers from their consumers through an event channel — publishers announce events without knowing who receives them — so new consumers can be added, removed or redeployed without changing the producer.
problem: One component's state change or announcement concerns several independent consumers (another module, the UI, a cache, an audit log), the set of consumers is dynamic and changes independently of the producer, and wiring direct calls from producer to consumer would hard-wire identity, ordering and failure behaviour into the producer. The recurring decision is therefore how to broadcast the event to an unknown, changing set of interested parties; the catalog's use-when cell states it as decoupled multi-consumer notification, noting that at part level a Mediator or Observer usually suffices.
context: Event-driven communication inside one process or across a middleware boundary: producers publish named events or topics and consumers register interest in the ones they handle. It fits when the number and identity of consumers is unknown to the producer, when the same event must reach several consumers with different reactions, or when producers and consumers are deployed, scaled or restarted independently. Component-local parts with a fixed subscriber set are better served by Observer or a Mediator, which keeps the collaboration graph explicit.
benefits: Publishers are unaware of consumers: new subscribers are added or removed by registering with the channel, without editing or redeploying the producer.
One-to-many broadcast is first-class: a single publication reaches every interested subscriber, each reacting independently.
Subscribers evolve independently: the channel hides their identity, number and location, so they can be developed, tested and deployed on their own schedule.
Temporal decoupling: with an asynchronous or buffered channel, slow, restarting or temporarily absent subscribers do not stop the publisher.
Filtering belongs to the channel: topic or content-based selection keeps consumers from handling events they do not care about, and keeps topic knowledge out of the producer.
Testability: an in-process channel can be replaced by a recording subscriber, so producers and consumers are exercised in isolation.
Horizontal scalability: brokered pub/sub (Kafka, SNS, Pub/Sub) allows independent consumer groups to scale horizontally without affecting the publisher or other consumer groups.
Polyglot integration: any language or platform that can connect to the broker can publish or subscribe, enabling heterogeneous system integration.
tradeoffs: Control flow becomes indirect: the publisher cannot see who reacts, and a missing or silent subscriber looks exactly like a working one, so tracing an event's effects needs correlation ids or logging.

Delivery semantics are undefined until you choose them: an in-process channel delivers at most once to whoever is subscribed at that instant, so events published before subscribe or while a subscriber is down are simply lost — the same decoupling is what makes delivery hard to guarantee.

The channel becomes a shared coupling point and a single point of failure: every participant depends on the bus and on the event contract, and the bus itself must be versioned, tested and kept available.

A synchronous dispatch lets one slow or throwing subscriber stall or break the publisher's path; an asynchronous dispatch trades that for unbounded queues, and both need an explicit overflow and error policy.
Subscription lifecycle is a leak risk: listeners held strongly keep dead objects alive, and handlers that are never unsubscribed keep receiving events.
Identity decoupling does not decouple the contract: the event's name, shape and semantics are shared by every subscriber, so schema changes break consumers silently.
Backpressure can be invisible: with push-based brokers, a slow consumer cannot apply backpressure to the publisher; the broker buffers indefinitely until memory is exhausted.

False ordering guarantees: global message ordering across all partitions is expensive and typically impractical at scale; assuming ordering when only per-key ordering is guaranteed leads to subtle data inconsistencies.

Operational complexity: a brokered deployment introduces infrastructure provisioning, monitoring, replication, schema registry, and consumer-group lag tracking that an in-process channel does not require.
Vendor lock-in risk: managed broker services (AWS SNS/SQS, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Azure Event Hubs) impose APIs, semantics and limits that migrating away from is costly.

participants.responsibility: Detects the state change or announcement, builds the event and hands it to the channel; knows only the channel's publish operation and the event contract.
Registers interest in one or more event classes or topics and handles the matching events; owns its own failure, retry and idempotency behaviour.
The immutable notification (topic or type plus payload) that carries everything a subscriber needs; the only contract shared by publisher and subscriber.
Accepts publications, maintains the subscription registry and hands each event to the subscribers whose interest matches.
Derives the routing key from the event (topic, event type or content) and decides which registered subscriptions match it.
Delivers selected events through the chosen mechanism — synchronous call, queue or thread pool — keeping publisher and subscribers decoupled in time as well as identity.
Handle returned by subscribe; removing or cancelling it closes the registration and releases the subscriber's listener state.

use_cases: In-process application events: a domain module announces OrderPlaced and the invoicing, shipping, audit and notification modules react without the ordering module knowing any of them.
Plugin and extension systems: the host publishes lifecycle events (on-load, on-request, on-shutdown) and plugins subscribe to the ones they implement, discovered at runtime.
UI and store fan-out: a document or store publishes change events, and several views, the status bar and the undo history subscribe to what they render.
Cache, metrics and tracing subscribers consuming the same domain events as business consumers (invalidation, counters, spans) without the publisher carrying that code.
Telemetry and device gateways: a reader publishes every reading to a logger, a dashboard and a persistence sink that may lag, restart or be added later.
Cross-service integration over a broker: each service publishes to a topic (Kafka, Redis Pub/Sub, SNS, Google Cloud Pub/Sub) and every interested consumer group receives a copy at its own pace.

IoT sensor telemetry: MQTT brokers distribute temperature, pressure and vibration readings from plant floor devices to SCADA historians, alarm handlers and ML anomaly detectors, each on their own subscription.

Event-driven microservices: an order service publishes order.created and shipping, invoicing, fraud detection, and email notification services each process the event independently from their own consumer group.

Real-time collaborative editing: a document service broadcasts cursor moves, edits and presence updates to all active sessions via a low-latency pub/sub channel so participants see each other's changes instantly.

Financial audit trails: a trading platform publishes trade-executed and position-change events to an immutable topic consumed by compliance, risk management, and reconciliation systems in separate consumer groups.

Notification systems at scale: Netflix's Rapid Event Notification System (RENO) subscribes to events from dozens of microservices and fans out to millions of heterogeneous devices (iOS, Android, smart TVs, web) via a hybrid push-pull model — the publisher remains unaware of device-specific delivery logic.

Real-time push messaging: Uber's RAMEN system maintains millions of persistent WebSocket connections and uses pub/sub internally to route ride status updates, driver offers and delivery ETAs with sub-10 ms end-to-end latency across a globally distributed fleet.

Platform-wide event backbone: Uber runs Apache Kafka as the central event bus handling trillions of messages per day across thousands of topics, with a Consumer Proxy (uForwarder) layer that presents a gRPC interface to services, hiding Kafka consumer group complexity and enabling independent service scaling.

Apache Kafka topic fan-out: independent consumer groups subscribe to the same topic so each logical subscriber receives the full event stream, while members within one group share partitions and offsets for scalable processing and replay.

Amazon SNS topic fan-out: a publisher sends once to an SNS topic and the service delivers to subscribed endpoints such as SQS queues, with subscription filter policies and protocol-specific payloads for independently evolving consumers.
avoid_when: One fixed consumer: a direct call (or an Observer relationship with a known subject) is simpler and keeps the control flow visible.
The caller needs an answer: pub/sub is one-way — use a direct call, a Future/Promise or Request-Reply instead of bolting correlation onto events.
Ordering or exactly-once delivery is required: a queue with acknowledgements (Point-to-Point Channel, Guaranteed Delivery) is the honest tool, not a broadcast channel.
The consumers are not actually independent — they share the publisher's transaction or need its in-memory state: hidden coupling through the bus will surface as inconsistent state.
A handful of listeners are all known at construction time: Mediator or Observer keep that graph explicit and debuggable; the channel only adds indirection.

Strong consistency across all consumers is required within a single transaction: pub/sub provides eventual consistency; if all consumers must see the same state atomically, a synchronous mechanism with distributed transactions (Saga with orchestration) is more appropriate.

The network boundary introduces unacceptable latency for the publisher's workflow: brokered pub/sub adds at minimum network round-trip latency; if the publisher blocks waiting for consumer results, the decoupling benefit is lost.
anti_patterns: Global event bus as a hidden singleton: anything can publish or subscribe to anything, dependencies become invisible and the bus degenerates into a service locator with an event-shaped API.
Event soup: hundreds of undocumented event names shared process-wide, so no one can tell a producer's consumers from a subscriber's producers.
Re-entrant notification storms: a subscriber publishes the same or a derived event inside its handler without a guard, producing feedback loops or infinite recursion.
Using pub/sub for request/response: ignoring that the pattern is one-way, then bolting correlation, timeouts and reply channels onto it instead of using Request-Reply.
Fire-and-forget for critical work with no delivery policy: assuming events are persisted or retried when the in-process channel does neither, so work silently goes missing.
Reaching for a broker where a callback would do: decoupling two objects that live in the same class, which just inflates the design.
Assuming ordering is guaranteed when it is not: publishing events that depend on each other on a channel that does not preserve order, then debugging why consumers see an earlier state.

Mixing command and event semantics on the same topic: publishing both Command events (do this) and Domain Events (this happened) to the same channel so subscribers cannot distinguish side effects from notifications.
Retaining unbounded backlogs without consumer groups: a slow consumer causes an unlimited queue to grow until memory is exhausted, crashing the broker or publisher.
Publishing mutable shared state: sending live objects or references that subscribers can modify, causing hidden cross-subscriber interference and non-deterministic behaviour.

Event Notification masquerading as Event Carried State Transfer: publishing thin notification events that force every subscriber to make a synchronous fetch to reconstruct state, creating tight runtime coupling hidden behind an event-shaped API.

Notification callback storm: a thin event triggers downstream subscribers to all query the same data source simultaneously, spiking load on the publisher's storage at the exact moment the event fires.
God Consumer: a single subscriber that knows about and handles too many event types, becoming a monolithic aggregator that defeats the purpose of decoupling.
Event Schema Spaghetti: implicit, unversioned event schemas that drift silently as publishers evolve, causing runtime failures in subscribers that have not been co-deployed.
Chatty Event Storm: publishing every tiny state change as a separate event, creating cascades of related events that overwhelm consumers and obscure meaningful business signals.
Event-Driven Monolith: loose-looking asynchronous decoupling that collapses into a synchronous event loop where every component depends on every other, losing all scalability benefit.
Silent data loss through TTL expiry: relying on ephemeral in-memory pub/sub with no persistence, losing events published while a subscriber is temporarily disconnected.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: publisher and subscriber depend on the channel's publish/subscribe abstraction and the event contract, not on each other.
Open/closed principle: new consumers arrive by subscription, without modifying the publisher.
Separation of concerns: routing and delivery belong to the channel; business reactions belong to the subscribers.
Loose coupling (Law of Demeter): the publisher talks to one channel instead of to every consumer it may ever have.
Single responsibility: the channel owns subscription bookkeeping and dispatch policy — it must not accumulate business logic.
Interface segregation on the subscriber side: each subscriber registers only for the event types it actually handles, not a generic catch-all.
Event immutability: events are immutable once published; any mutation happens in the subscriber before it produces its own derived events.
Contract stability: the event schema is a shared API; evolve it through versioning and backward compatibility, never through in-place changes.
Idempotency by default: since at-least-once delivery is the most common broker guarantee, every subscriber must tolerate duplicate messages gracefully.
best_practices: Name events as things that happened (past tense), version the payload schema, and treat events as immutable snapshots — never publish live entities that subscribers can mutate.
Return and store an unsubscribe handle from every subscription; call it deterministically on teardown (shutdown, unmount, scope exit) to prevent listener leaks and zombie deliveries.

Isolate subscriber failures: catch per-subscriber, log or route to a dead-letter/invalid-event path, and continue dispatching remaining subscribers — never let one subscriber's exception propagate to the publisher.

Choose and document the channel's delivery semantics explicitly: at-most-once (fire-and-forget), at-least-once (acknowledged delivery), or exactly-once (deduplicated). Mismatch between publisher assumption and subscriber expectation is the leading cause of silent data loss.
Scope the bus deliberately: prefer one instance injected as a dependency over a process-wide singleton, and keep topic/event names in one place (constants, a typed event map, or a registry).
Keep events small and cheap to copy: publish references or IDs to immutable payloads rather than deep-copying large objects per subscriber.
Apply content or topic-based filtering at the channel level so subscribers receive only events they handle — avoid broadcasting everything and relying on subscribers to ignore what they don't want.

Design for idempotent consumers: since at-least-once delivery is the most common guarantee, every subscriber must tolerate duplicate messages gracefully (use event IDs, version vectors, or database unique constraints).
For brokered pub/sub (Kafka, SNS, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ): use separate subscriptions per consumer group, not shared subscriptions — each group receives a full copy independently.
Prefer topic exchanges with routing-key or content-based filters over fanout-to-queue when subscriber sets overlap, to avoid routing duplication and maintenance overhead.
When using MQTT: choose QoS level deliberately — QoS 0 for high-frequency non-critical telemetry, QoS 1 for most industrial data including alarms, QoS 2 only when exactly-once is genuinely required.

Retain a sensible number of messages in the channel during subscriber downtime: brokered channels with message retention (Kafka, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, Redis Streams) allow late-joining subscribers to replay missed events.
Use correlation IDs on every event: propagate a correlationId (and optionally a causationId) so distributed traces can reconstruct the full event chain across service boundaries.

Define a dead-letter strategy before you need it: when a message cannot be delivered or processed after N retries, route it to a DLQ with enough context (error type, original payload, retry count) for later triage.

Avoid publishing to multiple topics that represent a single logical workflow: a single topic with typed payload discriminators (or a schema registry with evolved event types) is easier to govern than cross-referencing N topics.
For Kafka: use key-based partitioning when related events must be processed in order by the same consumer; understand that partition count limits parallel consumer concurrency.
For Redis Pub/Sub: treat it as ephemeral and fire-and-forget — it has no message persistence, no replay, and no consumer-group tracking; use Redis Streams when you need those guarantees.
When mixing pub/sub with request/reply in the same system: use separate channels or topics for each pattern; mixing them on one bus obscures which consumers can block and which cannot.
Instrument consumer lag: track the time between publish and delivery for each consumer group; a lagging subscriber is a silent failure mode that compounds during outages.

Enforce schema validation at the broker: use a schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry, AWS Glue, CloudEvents) to reject events that do not conform to the registered schema, preventing schema drift from propagating to consumers.
